sections.label: Origins and early generations
sections.note: Genesis opens with creation and human disobedience, then follows Cain, Noah’s flood, the generations after him, and the scattering at Babel.

sections.label: Abraham and his household
sections.note: God calls Abram and makes covenant promises; the stories follow Sarah, Lot, Hagar, Isaac’s birth, and the next generation in Abraham’s household.

sections.label: Isaac, Jacob, and Esau
sections.note: Isaac’s household gives way to Jacob’s flight, marriages, children, and return; the section closes with Jacob and Esau’s encounter and Esau’s descendants.

sections.label: Joseph is sold
sections.note: Joseph’s dreams deepen the brothers’ resentment, and they sell him to traders carrying him toward Egypt.

sections.label: Judah’s household
sections.note: Judah leaves his brothers, while Tamar’s actions expose his failure to honor his promise and preserve the family line through Perez and Zerah.

sections.label: Joseph in Egypt
sections.note: Sold into Egypt, Joseph serves in Potiphar’s house and prison before interpreting Pharaoh’s dreams and being appointed to oversee food supplies.

sections.label: Joseph and his family in Egypt
sections.note: Joseph tests and then recognizes his brothers; Jacob’s family settles in Egypt, and Jacob and Joseph both die after speaking about the promised land.

sections.label: Israel in Egypt
sections.note: Israel’s growth is followed by forced labor under Pharaoh; Moses is called, and the plagues culminate in Passover and the people’s departure.

sections.label: Departure and wilderness episodes
sections.note: After leaving Egypt, Israel crosses the sea and faces hunger, thirst, and battle in the wilderness; Moses also receives practical counsel from Jethro.

sections.label: Covenant at Sinai
sections.note: At Sinai, the people hear the covenant commands and laws, agree to the covenant, and Moses confirms it before going up the mountain.

sections.label: Tabernacle instructions
sections.note: These chapters give instructions for the tabernacle, its furnishings, priestly garments, and the consecration of Aaron and his sons.

sections.label: Covenant rupture and renewal
sections.note: While Moses is on the mountain, Israel makes a golden calf; Moses intercedes, and the covenant is renewed after the people’s breach.

sections.label: The tabernacle is made
sections.note: The people bring materials and build the tabernacle as instructed; when it is set up, the cloud and the LORD’s glory fill it.

sections.label: Offerings and priestly instructions
sections.note: The opening chapters describe offerings and specify how priests and worshippers are to present them.

sections.label: Priests are consecrated
sections.note: Aaron and his sons are ordained, but Nadab and Abihu die after bringing unauthorized fire before the LORD.

sections.label: Purity laws
sections.note: These chapters distinguish clean and unclean foods and address childbirth, skin conditions, and bodily discharges.

sections.label: The Day of Atonement
sections.note: The high priest enters the sanctuary with prescribed offerings, and the scapegoat carries the people’s iniquities into the wilderness.

sections.label: Holiness and priestly duties
sections.note: The text regulates blood, worship, sexual conduct, justice, and the responsibilities and limits of the priests.

sections.label: Festivals and land provisions
sections.note: Israel’s calendar of appointed feasts is set out alongside sabbath years, land provisions, and the Jubilee.

sections.label: Covenant outcomes and vows
sections.note: The covenant blessings and curses are stated, followed by instructions on vows, dedicated persons, property, and tithes.

sections.label: The camp is organized at Sinai
sections.note: The census, camp arrangement, and Levite duties prepare Israel to leave Sinai, where the tabernacle cloud signals when to travel.

sections.label: Complaints and the spies
sections.note: Complaints spread through the camp, Miriam and Aaron challenge Moses, and the spies’ report leads the people to refuse entry into Canaan.

sections.label: Laws and priestly episodes
sections.note: Further offerings and community rules accompany accounts of rebellion, priestly duties, and the red heifer’s purification rite.

sections.label: The journey toward Moab
sections.note: At Kadesh Miriam dies and Moses strikes the rock; Israel then moves toward Moab through conflict and battles on the way.

sections.label: Balaam and Moab
sections.note: Balak summons Balaam to curse Israel, but Balaam blesses them; the section ends with Israel’s unfaithfulness at Peor.

sections.label: A new census and instructions
sections.note: A new census prepares for settlement, while the daughters of Zelophehad, inheritance, offerings, festivals, and vows receive attention.

sections.label: The plains of Moab and inheritance
sections.note: Before crossing the Jordan, Israel fights Midian, assigns eastern lands, records the route and borders, and sets out inheritance and refuge rules.

sections.label: Moses reviews the journey
sections.note: Moses recounts the departure from Horeb, Israel’s refusal to enter the land, and the later victories east of the Jordan.

sections.label: Covenant and remembrance
sections.note: Moses repeats the covenant commands, calls Israel to love the LORD, and warns the people not to forget the God who brought them out of Egypt.

sections.label: Worship, justice, and festivals
sections.note: Israel receives laws for worship, festivals, tithes, and public justice, including the instruction to worship at the place the LORD chooses.

sections.label: Leaders and public duties
sections.note: The rules address courts, priests, prophets, kings, warfare, and cities of refuge, setting duties and limits for leaders and the community.

sections.label: Community laws
sections.note: These varied laws concern family obligations, laborers, property, honest measures, care for the vulnerable, and firstfruits and tithes.

sections.label: Covenant renewed at Moab
sections.note: At Moab, Moses sets out covenant blessings and curses and urges Israel to choose life by remaining faithful to the LORD.

sections.label: Joshua commissioned and Moses’ final words
sections.note: Moses commissions Joshua, gives Israel a song and blessing, and dies after viewing the land from afar.

sections.label: Preparation and the Jordan crossing
sections.note: Joshua is commissioned, spies meet Rahab, and Israel crosses the Jordan, setting up memorial stones to mark the passage.

sections.label: Campaign narratives
sections.note: The campaigns include Jericho, Ai, the Gibeonite treaty, and battles in the south and north as Israel takes cities in the land.

sections.label: The land is apportioned
sections.note: The remaining territories are assigned among the tribes, including the inheritance given to Caleb and the daughters of Zelophehad.

sections.label: Cities, Levites, and eastern tribes
sections.note: Israel appoints cities of refuge and Levitical towns; the eastern tribes’ altar nearly sparks conflict before they explain its purpose.

sections.label: Joshua’s farewell and covenant
sections.note: Joshua urges Israel to serve the LORD, renews the covenant at Shechem, and dies alongside Eleazar.

sections.label: The tribes and first deliverers
sections.note: After Joshua’s death, incomplete conquest is followed by repeated cycles of disobedience and deliverance, including the judges Othniel and Ehud.

sections.label: Deborah and Barak
sections.note: Deborah and Barak lead Israel against Sisera’s army, and Deborah’s song celebrates the victory.

sections.label: Gideon
sections.note: Gideon is called to confront Midian, wins with a reduced force, and later makes an ephod that becomes a snare to Israel.

sections.label: Abimelech and later judges
sections.note: Abimelech seizes power violently; later judges include Jephthah, whose vow and conflict with Ephraim shape the closing chapters of this section.

sections.label: Samson
sections.note: Samson’s birth is announced, and his conflicts with the Philistines lead to betrayal, capture, and his final attack on their gathering.

sections.label: Tribal conflict and disorder
sections.note: Micah’s images and Dan’s migration lead into the outrage at Gibeah, civil war, and the repeated disorder of Israel’s tribes.

sections.label: Naomi and Ruth return
sections.note: A famine brings Naomi’s family to Moab; after losing her husband and sons, Naomi returns to Bethlehem with Ruth, whose loyalty is central to the story.

sections.label: Ruth gleans in Boaz’s field
sections.note: Ruth gleans in Boaz’s field, and Boaz ensures she is protected and provided for.

sections.label: Ruth speaks with Boaz
sections.note: At Naomi’s direction, Ruth asks Boaz to act as a family redeemer; he agrees while acknowledging that a nearer relative has prior claim.

sections.label: The family is redeemed
sections.note: Boaz settles the matter at the town gate, marries Ruth, and becomes the father of Obed, whose line leads to David.

sections.label: Samuel’s birth and calling
sections.note: Hannah prays for a son and dedicates Samuel to the LORD; Samuel is called while Eli’s sons are condemned for their conduct.

sections.label: The ark and its return
sections.note: The Philistines capture the ark, but after calamity in their cities they return it; Israel turns back to the LORD under Samuel and wins at Mizpah.

sections.label: Israel asks for a king
sections.note: Israel asks for a king, Saul is anointed and publicly confirmed, and Samuel warns the people about the cost of kingship.

sections.label: Saul’s early reign
sections.note: Saul’s impatience and disobedience in battle lead Samuel to announce that the LORD has rejected him as king.

sections.label: David is chosen and Goliath falls
sections.note: Samuel anoints David, who enters Saul’s service and defeats Goliath when Israel’s army is challenged by the Philistines.

sections.label: David and Saul’s household
sections.note: Jonathan and David form a close bond, while Saul’s jealousy grows and David repeatedly escapes attempts on his life.

sections.label: David’s flight and Saul’s end
sections.note: David hides from Saul among wilderness refuges and Philistine territory; Saul and his sons fall in battle on Mount Gilboa.

sections.label: David becomes king in Judah
sections.note: After Saul’s death, David mourns Saul and Jonathan and becomes king over Judah, while conflict continues between the houses of Saul and David.

sections.label: Jerusalem and the ark
sections.note: David is made king over all Israel, captures Jerusalem, and brings the ark there, though Uzzah dies when he touches it.

sections.label: The kingdom and its promises
sections.note: God promises David an enduring house; the narrative then recounts David’s victories and his kindness to Mephibosheth.

sections.label: David and Bathsheba
sections.note: David takes Bathsheba and arranges Uriah’s death; Nathan confronts him, and the child dies before Solomon is born.

sections.label: Conflict within David’s household
sections.note: Amnon violates Tamar, Absalom kills Amnon and later rebels, forcing David to flee; Absalom dies in the ensuing battle.

sections.label: The kingdom is restored and final accounts
sections.note: David returns to power amid further unrest; the closing chapters recount a census and plague alongside songs, warriors, and final words.

sections.label: Solomon succeeds David
sections.note: Adonijah’s bid for the throne is stopped and Solomon is established as king; he asks God for wisdom and judges a disputed case.

sections.label: The Temple is built and dedicated
sections.note: Solomon builds and dedicates the Temple, prays for the people, and receives a promise concerning the house and covenant.

sections.label: Solomon’s wealth and decline
sections.note: The Queen of Sheba visits Solomon, whose wealth is displayed; his foreign wives turn his heart, and adversaries rise before his death.

sections.label: The kingdom divides
sections.note: Rehoboam rejects the people’s request and the kingdom divides; the account follows rival reigns in Israel and Judah through Ahab’s rise.

sections.label: Elijah and the drought
sections.note: Elijah announces drought, is sustained by a widow, confronts Baal’s prophets at Carmel, and later meets the LORD at Horeb.

sections.label: Ahab and the prophets
sections.note: Ahab fights Syria, covets Naboth’s vineyard, and hears Micaiah’s warning before he dies in battle.

sections.label: Elijah and Elisha
sections.note: Elijah’s ministry passes to Elisha, whose signs include healing Naaman, restoring a child, and helping during Israel’s conflicts and famine.

sections.label: Regime changes and Samaria falls
sections.note: Jehu’s revolt destroys Ahab’s house, but Israel’s rulers continue to change until Assyria captures Samaria and carries the people away.

sections.label: Hezekiah and Jerusalem
sections.note: Hezekiah reforms Judah and faces the Assyrian siege of Jerusalem; after recovery from illness, he receives envoys from Babylon.

sections.label: Judah’s decline and Josiah’s reform
sections.note: Manasseh’s long reign is followed by Josiah’s discovery of the law and sweeping reforms, though Josiah dies in battle.

sections.label: Jerusalem falls and exile begins
sections.note: Babylon deposes Judah’s kings, deports its people, and destroys Jerusalem and the Temple; the final verses note Jehoiachin’s release.

sections.label: Genealogies of Israel
sections.note: These genealogies trace families from Adam through Israel’s tribes and identify the Levites, priests, and residents of Jerusalem.

sections.label: Saul’s death and David’s rise
sections.note: Saul dies in battle, and David becomes king as warriors from across Israel gather to support him.

sections.label: The ark is brought to Jerusalem
sections.note: David organizes the ark’s journey to Jerusalem after Uzzah dies, then establishes Levites and musicians to lead worship there.

sections.label: David’s reign and the census
sections.note: God’s promise to David is followed by accounts of his victories, the census, and the plague that leads him to the Temple site.

sections.label: Preparation for the Temple
sections.note: David gathers materials, organizes Temple service, charges Solomon with the work, and gives thanks before his death.

sections.label: Solomon and the Temple
sections.note: Solomon asks for wisdom, builds and dedicates the Temple, and receives the Queen of Sheba as a visitor.

sections.label: Judah and the divided kingdom
sections.note: After the northern tribes break away under Rehoboam, the account follows Judah’s kings through Asa and Jehoshaphat, including their reforms and alliances.

sections.label: Judah’s kings and crises
sections.note: Judah’s later kings face coups, military crises, and damage to the Temple as the account contrasts their choices and reigns.

sections.label: Hezekiah’s reform
sections.note: Hezekiah cleanses the Temple, restores worship and Passover, and leads Judah through the Assyrian threat to Jerusalem.

sections.label: Manasseh, Josiah, and reform
sections.note: Manasseh later humbles himself after captivity, while Josiah repairs the Temple, hears the law, and leads a major reform before his death.

sections.label: Jerusalem falls and return is announced
sections.note: Judah’s final kings fall to Babylon, Jerusalem and the Temple are destroyed, and Cyrus’s decree opens the way for return.

sections.label: Return and altar restoration
sections.note: Cyrus permits the exiles to return, and the people rebuild the altar and lay the Temple foundation amid both celebration and grief.

sections.label: The Temple is rebuilt
sections.note: Opposition interrupts the work, but Haggai and Zechariah encourage the builders; a Persian decree confirms the project, which is completed.

sections.label: Ezra comes to Jerusalem
sections.note: Ezra receives authority from Artaxerxes, leads another group to Jerusalem, and entrusts the journey and its offerings to God.

sections.label: A communal crisis and response
sections.note: Ezra responds to reports of intermarriage with prayer and public confession, followed by an assembly that addresses the crisis.

sections.label: Nehemiah receives a commission
sections.note: After hearing that Jerusalem’s wall is broken, Nehemiah prays, obtains the king’s support, and surveys the city at night.

sections.label: The wall is repaired
sections.note: Families and tradespeople repair the wall despite threats; Nehemiah also confronts debt and exploitation, and the work is completed.

sections.label: The law is read and the people respond
sections.note: Ezra reads and explains the law, the people celebrate the Feast of Booths, confess their history, and renew their covenant commitments.

sections.label: Jerusalem’s community and reforms
sections.note: Residents are assigned to Jerusalem and the wall is dedicated; Nehemiah later corrects abuses involving the Temple, Sabbath, and marriage.

sections.label: Esther enters the Persian court
sections.note: After Vashti is removed, Esther is chosen as queen, and Mordecai uncovers a plot against the king.

sections.label: Haman’s decree and Esther’s decision
sections.note: Haman’s decree threatens the Jews; Mordecai urges Esther to act, and she risks approaching the king before arranging a banquet.

sections.label: The plot is reversed
sections.note: The king honors Mordecai after hearing the old record, Haman is executed, and Esther obtains a new decree to protect the Jews.

sections.label: Deliverance and Purim
sections.note: The Jews defend themselves from attack, Purim is established as a yearly observance, and Mordecai is elevated in the Persian court.

sections.label: The opening frame
sections.note: The story’s frame presents Job as upright, then depicts the accuser’s challenges and Job’s loss of children, property, and health.

sections.label: Job speaks and the first replies begin
sections.note: Job laments his birth, and his friends begin speeches that try to explain his suffering while Job protests and seeks an answer from God.

sections.label: The debate continues
sections.note: The debate continues as Job’s friends press their case and Job rejects their certainty about his guilt and appeals to God’s justice.

sections.label: Wisdom and Job’s defense
sections.note: A poem asks where wisdom can be found, then Job recalls his former standing and defends the integrity of his life.

sections.label: Elihu speaks
sections.note: Elihu criticizes both Job and the friends, arguing that God may use suffering to instruct and pointing to God’s power in the world.

sections.label: The LORD answers and Job’s story closes
sections.note: The LORD answers Job from the whirlwind; Job responds, the friends are rebuked, and Job’s fortunes are restored.

sections.label: Psalms, Book I
sections.note: The first collection opens by contrasting the way of the righteous and the wicked; Davidic laments, confessions, thanksgiving, and praise recur throughout.

sections.label: Psalms, Book II
sections.note: These psalms voice longing for God and refuge amid distress, include royal and communal prayers, and end with a prayer for the king’s just rule.

sections.label: Psalms, Book III
sections.note: Many psalms confront national disaster and the apparent failure of the Davidic promise, turning toward God’s sanctuary and past acts of deliverance.

sections.label: Psalms, Book IV
sections.note: The collection centers on the LORD’s kingship and human mortality, remembering Israel’s history and calling all creation to praise.

sections.label: Psalms, Book V
sections.note: Thanksgiving for deliverance, instruction in God’s law, songs for pilgrims, and repeated calls to praise bring the Psalter to its close.

sections.label: Wisdom’s instruction
sections.note: The opening instructions portray Wisdom calling in public and contrast her path with folly, violence, and sexual temptation.

sections.label: Sayings of Solomon
sections.note: Brief sayings associated with Solomon contrast wisdom and folly in speech, work, justice, family life, wealth, and rule.

sections.label: Sayings of the wise
sections.note: These sayings of the wise counsel restraint, honest dealing, care for the poor, and prudence around rulers and neighbors.

sections.label: Solomon’s sayings copied by Hezekiah’s men
sections.note: Hezekiah’s men copied these sayings of Solomon, which address self-control, leadership, conflict, fools, and justice.

sections.label: The words of Agur
sections.note: Agur reflects on human limits and God’s words, then uses numerical sayings to observe patterns in nature and human behavior.

sections.label: The words of Lemuel and the capable woman
sections.note: Lemuel’s mother counsels the king to defend the poor and avoid excess; the closing poem praises a capable woman and her work.

sections.label: The question of profit
sections.note: The Preacher tests pleasure, wisdom, labor, and wealth, asking what lasting gain people receive from their work.

sections.label: Time, labor, and limits
sections.note: A poem assigns seasons to human affairs, while the text considers injustice, toil, companionship, possessions, and the limits of control.

sections.label: Wisdom under uncertainty
sections.note: These reflections weigh wisdom against adversity and uncertainty, urging action while acknowledging that people cannot know or govern every outcome.

sections.label: Remember the Creator
sections.note: The closing chapter depicts aging and death and urges readers to remember their Creator; the conclusion calls them to fear God and keep his commandments.

sections.label: The speakers praise and desire
sections.note: The lovers exchange praise and desire, using images of gardens, fragrance, and the natural world to express their affection.

sections.label: Seeking and mutual praise
sections.note: The beloved searches for her lover, and the speakers praise one another’s beauty in a wedding-like procession and intimate poems.

sections.label: Absence and return
sections.note: After a delayed response and separation, the beloved searches for her lover; the poems return to mutual admiration and reunion.

sections.label: Love’s closing words
sections.note: The final songs celebrate desire and the strength of love, which cannot be bought or extinguished by many waters.

sections.label: Judah, Jerusalem, and the nations
sections.note: Isaiah indicts Judah and Jerusalem, recounts his call, and speaks of judgment and hope amid threats from neighboring powers.

sections.label: Oracles concerning the nations
sections.note: Oracles address Babylon, Moab, Egypt, Tyre, and other nations, warning that political power and alliances cannot secure them from judgment.

sections.label: Judgment and hope
sections.note: The earth is pictured under judgment, yet the text promises a feast on Zion, the defeat of death, and songs of trust.

sections.label: Warnings and promises
sections.note: Warnings against relying on Egypt and other powers are paired with promises that the redeemed will return along a way of holiness.

sections.label: Hezekiah and the Assyrian threat
sections.note: Assyria besieges Judah, Hezekiah prays and Jerusalem is spared; the king’s illness and Babylonian visitors point toward future exile.

sections.label: Comfort, servant passages, and return
sections.note: Words of comfort promise God’s power and a return from exile; the servant passages speak of suffering, justice, and restoration.

sections.label: Justice, worship, and renewal
sections.note: The closing chapters call for justice and faithful worship, challenge empty ritual, and envision renewed Zion and a new creation.

sections.label: Jeremiah is called and warnings begin
sections.note: Jeremiah receives his call and sees signs of coming danger; he indicts Israel and Judah for turning from the LORD and warns of invasion.

sections.label: The Temple sermon and covenant warning
sections.note: The Temple sermon rejects confidence in the building while the people persist in injustice and idolatry; Jeremiah grieves over the coming judgment.

sections.label: Covenant dispute and opposition
sections.note: Jeremiah confronts covenant-breaking and faces plots, imprisonment, and rejection as he delivers difficult messages to Judah.

sections.label: Kings, siege, and exile warnings
sections.note: Warnings to kings and people describe siege and exile; Jeremiah opposes false assurances and writes to exiles in Babylon.

sections.label: Promises of restoration
sections.note: Promises of restoration include a return to the land, a renewed people, and a new covenant written on the heart.

sections.label: Jerusalem under siege
sections.note: As Babylon presses Jerusalem, Jeremiah condemns injustice, recalls the Rechabites’ obedience, and suffers imprisonment and violence.

sections.label: Jerusalem falls and oracles follow
sections.note: Jerusalem falls, Jeremiah is taken to Egypt after Gedaliah’s murder, and the book closes with oracles against nations and a record of exile.

sections.label: The city mourns
sections.note: Jerusalem is pictured as a bereaved city, and the speaker mourns its loss of people, status, and comfort.

sections.label: The city’s destruction
sections.note: The poem describes the destruction of Zion and its sanctuary, placing the suffering within a plea for God to look upon the people.

sections.label: Suffering and hope
sections.note: Amid intense affliction, the speaker remembers God’s mercies and urges waiting; the poem also gives voice to the community’s suffering.

sections.label: The siege remembered
sections.note: The poem recalls famine and siege, the ruin of the sanctuary, and the humiliation of the people and their leaders.

sections.label: A communal plea
sections.note: The final chapter is a communal plea that asks God to remember the people and restore them after their reproach.

sections.label: Ezekiel’s vision and call
sections.note: Ezekiel sees the LORD’s glory in a vision by the river Chebar and is commissioned to speak to the exiles as a watchman.

sections.label: Signs and judgment concerning Jerusalem
sections.note: Enacted signs portray Jerusalem under siege; visions of idolatry and judgment culminate in the glory of the LORD departing the Temple.

sections.label: Warnings before the fall
sections.note: Ezekiel warns that Jerusalem’s fall is near through sign-acts and oracles about the people’s unfaithfulness and coming judgment.

sections.label: Oracles concerning neighboring nations
sections.note: Oracles announce judgment on Ammon, Moab, Edom, Philistia, Tyre, Sidon, and Egypt for their violence and pride.

sections.label: Watchman, restoration, and hope
sections.note: At the news of Jerusalem’s fall, Ezekiel renews his watchman’s charge, condemns failed shepherds, and speaks of restoration, dry bones, and a final conflict.

sections.label: The temple vision
sections.note: A vision measures a restored Temple and land, with ordered worship, tribal allotments, and a river flowing from the sanctuary.

sections.label: Daniel and his companions in exile
sections.note: Daniel and his companions are taken to Babylon, remain faithful in the royal court, and Daniel explains Nebuchadnezzar’s dream of kingdoms.

sections.label: Stories at the imperial court
sections.note: Stories of the furnace, royal dreams, the writing on the wall, and the lions’ den show faithful servants facing imperial power.

sections.label: Daniel’s visions
sections.note: Daniel’s visions use beasts and heavenly figures to portray successive kingdoms, judgment, and the distress and deliverance of God’s people.

sections.label: Hosea’s family as a sign
sections.note: Hosea’s marriage and children become signs of Israel’s unfaithfulness, while the text also holds out hope of renewed relationship.

sections.label: Covenant accusation
sections.note: The prophet accuses Israel of covenant betrayal, corrupt worship, failed leadership, and misplaced reliance on political alliances.

sections.label: Judgment and compassion
sections.note: God recalls loving Israel from Egypt and grieves over judgment; the book ends by calling the people to return and promising healing.

sections.label: The land is devastated
sections.note: A devastating locust plague strips the land and leads Joel to call priests and people to lament and fast.

sections.label: A day of warning and promise
sections.note: The prophet announces the day of the LORD, calls the people to return, and promises restoration and the outpouring of God’s Spirit.

sections.label: The nations and restoration
sections.note: The nations are summoned for judgment while Judah’s restoration and the LORD’s presence in Zion are promised.

sections.label: Oracles against nations
sections.note: Amos announces judgment on surrounding nations before turning to Judah and Israel for their own violence and injustice.

sections.label: Warnings to Israel
sections.note: Israel is called to account for oppression and false worship; the prophet urges the people to seek good and let justice flow.

sections.label: Visions and a promise of restoration
sections.note: Visions of locusts, fire, a plumb line, and ripe fruit warn of Israel’s end, while the book closes with a promise of restoration.

sections.label: A vision concerning Edom
sections.note: Obadiah condemns Edom’s pride and its violence against Judah, then looks toward the day when the LORD’s kingdom will be established.

sections.label: Jonah is sent toward Nineveh
sections.note: Jonah flees from the mission to Nineveh, and a storm at sea ends with the sailors casting him overboard.

sections.label: Jonah prays from the fish
sections.note: From inside the fish, Jonah prays for deliverance and is brought back to dry land.

sections.label: Jonah goes to Nineveh
sections.note: Sent again, Jonah warns Nineveh; its people repent, and God relents from the announced disaster.

sections.label: Jonah outside the city
sections.note: Jonah resents Nineveh’s reprieve, and the plant, worm, and wind expose his concern for himself beside God’s concern for the city.

sections.label: Judgment and lament
sections.note: Micah’s messages against Samaria and Jerusalem name coming judgment and lament the loss and oppression affecting the land.

sections.label: Leaders judged and hope announced
sections.note: The prophet condemns corrupt rulers and prophets, then sets judgment beside promises of peace and a ruler from Bethlehem.

sections.label: The covenant case and hope
sections.note: God brings a covenant case against the people, calls for justice and mercy, and the book ends with trust in God’s compassion.

sections.label: An oracle against Nineveh
sections.note: Nahum portrays the LORD as judge of Nineveh and comfort to Judah, announcing the city’s coming defeat.

sections.label: Nineveh’s fall described
sections.note: The final chapter condemns Nineveh’s violence and deceit, depicts the city’s collapse, and declares that its wound will not be healed.

sections.label: The prophet’s first complaint
sections.note: Habakkuk asks why violence and injustice go unanswered, then questions why God would use the ruthless Chaldeans as an instrument of judgment.

sections.label: The answer and the woes
sections.note: The prophet waits for God’s answer, hears that pride will not endure, and records woes against violence, exploitation, and idols.

sections.label: A prayer in poetic form
sections.note: Habakkuk’s prayer recalls God’s power and ends in trust and rejoicing even if crops and herds fail.

sections.label: The day of the LORD announced
sections.note: Zephaniah warns Judah that the day of the LORD will expose idolatry and complacency and bring judgment on Jerusalem.

sections.label: Warnings to nations
sections.note: The prophet calls the humble to seek the LORD and announces judgment on Philistia, Moab, Ammon, Cush, and Assyria.

sections.label: Judgment and restoration
sections.note: Jerusalem’s corrupt leaders are condemned, but the closing words promise a purified people and rejoicing in the LORD’s presence.

sections.label: The call to rebuild
sections.note: Haggai challenges the returned community for neglecting the Temple while tending their own houses; Zerubbabel and Joshua lead the rebuilding.

sections.label: Encouragement and promise
sections.note: The prophet encourages the builders, promises the Temple’s future glory, and gives Zerubbabel a sign of God’s choice.

sections.label: The night visions
sections.note: Zechariah calls the people to return to God, then recounts night visions about Jerusalem, Joshua the priest, Zerubbabel, judgment, and renewal.

sections.label: Fasting, justice, and hope
sections.note: A question about fasting leads to warnings against injustice and promises that Jerusalem will again be a place of peace and worship.

sections.label: Oracles and visions of the future
sections.note: These oracles speak of a humble king, a pierced figure and struck shepherd, Jerusalem’s trials, and the LORD’s final reign.

sections.label: Questions about worship and covenant
sections.note: Malachi condemns corrupt offerings and priestly failures, then confronts unfaithfulness in marriage and neglect of justice.

sections.label: The messenger and refiner
sections.note: The coming messenger and refiner announce judgment; the people are called to return to God, and the faithful are remembered.

sections.label: The coming day
sections.note: The final chapter warns of a coming day of judgment and promises healing, while urging Israel to remember Moses’ teaching.
